_comment: The ten Indian languages of SIH PS-26173, and where their models come from.
DATA, not code: the app reads this to decide what it can offer to download.
Adding an eleventh language is an edit to this file plus a pack.json, with no
Kotlin change anywhere — the same rule the rest of the project follows.
Recognition is AI4Bharat IndicConformer, Apache-2.0, one CTC graph per language
over a vocabulary SHARED by all ten. That sharing is why a second Indic language
costs only its own model file and not another 66 KB of tokens.
Speech: Piper/Mimic3 for en hi ml te gu, Meta MMS for ta mr kn or bn. Note the licence: CC-BY-NC 4.0, non-commercial only. That is
fine for a competition entry and must be stated; a commercial deployment needs a
different voice. Recognition carries no such restriction.

_why: One archive per language: model.onnx, tokens.txt, voice.json, and espeak-ng-data
for phoneme voices. Built by tools/package-voices.py.
voiceVersion is compared with the one recorded in an installed pack. Anything older
- including every voice from before it existed - is offered as an update. The v1
voices are the low-CPU builds: the previous int8 Tamil voice cost 15.7 s of CPU per
second of speech, and v1 costs about 0.6.
Licences: MMS voices (ta mr kn or bn) are CC-BY-NC 4.0, non-commercial. Piper and
Mimic3 voices (en hi ml te gu) follow their upstream model cards.

_idComment: The id is part of the frozen wire format (LanguageId / TRD section 4.3) and the
app resolves it from the ISO code below. Writing the numbers here as well would
mean two sources of truth for something that can never be renumbered — and the
first draft of this file got six of the ten WRONG, which would have put the wrong
language id on the wire for Bengali, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam
and Odia. A packet is supposed to decode to the same language in ten years.
